entries.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
entries.lesson_core_move: State the value-based definition of the unit step function and interpret it as the basic continuous-time on-off signal used to build shifted, delayed, and rectangular-pulse signal descriptions.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Introduction to Definition of the Unit Step Function

blocks.text: Introduce the unit step as the continuous-time switch function. In this lesson, we use it to indicate which time side of the axis is active and which side is off.
Teach the rule for times before the switch: for $t<0$, the switch is off, so $u(t)=0$.
Teach the rule for times after the switch: for $t>0$, the switch is on, so $u(t)=1$.
Use one base case to show both sides: if $t=-1$, then $u(-1)=0$, and if $t=2$, then $u(2)=1$.
Set the course convention at the boundary by declaring $u(0)=1$ for this topic line and using that same convention everywhere in this module.
This definition is the core building block for shifted and delayed step functions, and later it will be used to construct rectangular pulses and other on-off signal forms.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step Before and After the Switch

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $u(-4)$ and $u(3)$ with the definition from the tutorial.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the unit-step rule as the guide: for $t<0$, the signal is off and $u(t)=0$, and for $t>0$, the signal is on and $u(t)=1$.
Classify the first query: $-4<0$, so it is on the left side of the switch.
Apply the left-side rule to the query and report the result: $u(-4)=0$.
Classify the second query: $3>0$, so it is on the right side of the switch.
Apply the right-side rule and report the result: $u(3)=1$.
Final answer: $u(-4)=0$, $u(3)=1$. In this lesson format, any non-boundary point is solved by that same two-step pointwise classification and substitution pattern.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Unit Step at the Switching Time

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $u(0)$ and decide whether it differs from both one-sided limits.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same switch rule as the earlier sections: for $t<0$, $u(t)=0$, and for $t>0$, $u(t)=1$. The new cue here is to handle the boundary-time case.
Recognize $t=0$ is not a strict interior point, so it is not covered by either the left-hand or right-hand branch alone.
Apply the lesson convention directly at the boundary: $u(0)=1$ for this topic line.
For contrast, the neighbor values are $u(0^-)=0$ and $u(0^+)=1$ under the previously learned rules.
Result: the boundary point is $u(0)=1$, which does differ from the left-limit value at zero and matches the chosen on-value convention used in this lesson.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Reading the Unit Step Function from a Time-Axis Graph

image_slots.image_description: A time-axis graph of a binary unit-step function showing a constant 0 level for left-side times and a constant 1 level for right-side times, with a single jump at a marked switching instant. Include clear axis labels, horizontal segments only, and a visible switch marker.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the graph and compute $u(t)$ for three selected times, including the switch instant.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the graph as the cue: identify the switching instant first, then read which side of the jump each query time is on.
If the switch is at $t=0$, then the left-side region is $t<0$ and the right-side region is $t>0$.
Classify the selected times: $t=-2$ lies left of the switch, so $u(-2)=0$.
For the switch instant $t=0$, apply the lesson convention, so $u(0)=1$. In this lesson that is the same boundary convention used in symbolic work.
For $t=2$, the time is right of the jump, so $u(2)=1$. Therefore the on interval is $t\ge 0$ and the off interval is $t<0$ under this convention.

sections.lesson_title: Definition of the Unit Step Function
sections.section_title: Recognizing the Unit Step as the Basic Continuous-Time Switching Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite and interpret the piecewise signal defined by $x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=t^2$.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue that multiplication by $u(t)$ gates the signal by time region, so $x(t)u(t)$ must be split by the same $u(t)$ regions.
From the learned rule, if $t<0$, then $u(t)=0$, so $x(t)u(t)=t^2\cdot 0=0$ on the off region.
For $t>0$, the on region has $u(t)=1$, so $x(t)u(t)=t^2\cdot 1=t^2$ there.
Using the lesson convention at the boundary, $u(0)=1$, so $x(0)u(0)=0^2\cdot 1=0$ and the boundary aligns with the right-side expression.

entries.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret x(t)u(t) as using the unit step as an on-off switch that suppresses a continuous-time signal before t = 0 and passes it afterward, supporting construction of started, delayed, and pulsed signals with unit steps.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Introduction to Unit Step as an On-Off Switch

blocks.text: The object to recognize is the continuous-time unit step $u(t)$. In this topic, treat it as a switch: for $t<0$, it turns off; for $t\ge 0$, it turns on. Therefore a product $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ is a regionwise product that depends on the sign of $t$.
Use the base case $x(t)=1$ so the switch action is transparent: then $y(t)=u(t)$. For any $x(t)$, apply the same rule and write the decomposition explicitly as a switched expression.

The meaning is direct: $u(t)$ suppresses the signal before the switch time, so $y(t)=0$ for $t<0$, and it lets the original form pass unchanged afterward, so $y(t)=x(t)$ for $t\ge 0$. This same template will be reused as the core move whenever step multiplication defines a region of activation.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Evaluating x(t)u(t) Before t = 0

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ for $y(t)=(2-t)u(t)$ at $t=-1$.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: this is an on-off switch evaluation in the pre-switch region. Use $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=2-t$ and evaluate both factors at $t=-1$.
Because the switch is off in the region $t<0$, the value rule gives $u(-1)=0$.
Substitute that factor into the product: $y(-1)=(2-(-1))\cdot 0=0$. The result is $y(-1)=0$, which is exactly the explicit zero output in the blocked region.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Evaluating x(t)u(t) After t = 0

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $y(t)=(3t+1)u(t)$ at $t=2$.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: this is an on-region evaluation where the gate is open. Identify the target expression as $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ and substitute $t=2$ into both factors.
From the switch rule, for $t>0$, $u(t)=1$, so here $u(2)=1$.
Now compute the switched value directly: $y(2)=(3\cdot2+1)\cdot 1=7$. This matches the active formula $x(2)=7$, so in the on region $y(t)=x(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as an On-Off Switch
sections.section_title: Writing the On-Off Output of x(t)u(t) in Piecewise Form

example_content.example_prompt: Express $y(t)=(4t+1)u(t)$ as an explicit piecewise function of $t$.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: this is the same switch rule from earlier, now written for all times. Start from the generic product form $y(t)=x(t)u(t)$ with $x(t)=4t+1$.
Set the off branch using $t<0\Rightarrow u(t)=0$, and the on branch using $t\ge 0\Rightarrow u(t)=1$.
This form is explicit for every time region: $y(t)$ is blocked to zero before the switch and equals $x(t)$ after and at the switch point, which is the core on-off behavior of $x(t)u(t)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate shifted unit step functions into exact switch-on times on the continuous-time axis so they can be used to start, delay, and construct signals compactly.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Introduction to Shifted Unit Step Functions

blocks.text: The object to recognize in this step is the unit-step argument. In this topic, the rule is: the switch-on instant is the time that makes the argument of $u(\cdot)$ equal to zero.
Start from the base case. The canonical unit step is defined by $u(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $u(t)=1$ for $t\ge 0$, so the switch flips on at $t=0$.
For the shifted form $u(t-T)$, solve $t-T=0$ to get the switch-on time $t=T$. That means $u(t-T)=0$ for $t<T$ and $u(t-T)=1$ for $t\ge T$.
Now contrast with $u(t+T)$. Set $t+T=0$, so the switch occurs at $t=-T$. For positive $T$, this is an advance: the function turns on before zero.
Use the same rule for any shift: in $u(t-t_0)$, the switch-on time is $t=t_0$. Do not introduce a new formula here—only change the solve-and-substitute step.
Across this lesson, future steps will keep this template unchanged and vary only the inside offset. The action is always: set the inside argument to zero and identify the resulting on-time.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t - T)

example_content.example_prompt: Find the switch-on time of $y(t)=u(t-3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the argument inside $u(\cdot)$: here it is $t-3$. For a shifted step, the function switches on when this argument becomes zero.
Solve the condition directly: $t-3=0 \implies t=3$.
So $u(t-3)$ turns on at $t=3$. Therefore the signal is $y(t)=0$ for $t<3$ and $y(t)=1$ for $t\ge3$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t + T)

example_content.example_prompt: Find the switch-on time of $y(t)=u(t+2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the argument of the unit step: here it is $t+2$. Use the same rule as the previous section and set that argument to zero.
Solve for the switch-on time: $t+2=0 \implies t=-2$.
So this function switches on at $t=-2$. It is off before the switch and on at and after it: $y(t)=0$ for $t<-2$ and $y(t)=1$ for $t\ge-2$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Finding the Switch-On Time from u(t - t0)

example_content.example_prompt: If $y(t)=u(t-t_0)$ and $t_0=-1$, find the switch-on time.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted argument inside $u(\cdot)$: here it is $t-t_0$. Use the same rule and set that argument to zero.
Rearrange the equation to solve for the switch time: $t=t_0$.
Substitute the given value $t_0=-1$, so the switch-on time is $t=-1$.
The function is therefore $y(t)=0$ for $t<-1$ and $y(t)=1$ for $t\ge-1$.

sections.lesson_title: Shifted Unit Step Functions
sections.section_title: Placing Shifted Unit Steps on the Time Axis

image_slots.image_description: Draw a one-dimensional time axis with three vertical switch markers labeled with their signals: y1 at t=2 for u(t-2), y2 at t=-1 for u(t+1), and y3 at t=5 for u(t-5). Show only clean axis ticks, clear labels, and no grid.

example_content.example_prompt: Order the switch-on times of $y_1(t)=u(t-2)$, $y_2(t)=u(t+1)$, and $y_3(t)=u(t-5)$ from earliest to latest.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same cue as before: for each shifted step, set the inside of $u(\cdot)$ to zero and solve for the switch time.
Match each result to its function: $y_1$ switches at $2$, $y_2$ switches at $-1$, and $y_3$ switches at $5$.
Sort the switch times from earliest to latest: $-1 < 2 < 5$, so the ordering is $y_2$, $y_1$, $y_3$.

entries.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a zero-before-start continuous-time signal from piecewise form into a step-gated expression by multiplying the active formula by the unit step that turns on at the start time.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Introduction to Starting a Signal with a Unit Step

blocks.text: When a continuous-time signal is zero before a start time and follows one active formula after that time, the compact form is the active formula multiplied by a unit step. The unit step is the switch that marks where the signal turns on.

Think of the left side of the switch as the inactive interval and the right side as the active interval. In this lesson, the inactive side is $t<t_0$, the active side is $t\ge t_0$, and the step is what separates the two.
For the simplest case, place the switch at $t=0$. Then a signal that is $0$ for $t<0$ and $f(t)$ for $t\ge 0$ becomes a single gated expression.

For any later start time $t_0$, keep the active formula unchanged and shift only the step to $u(t-t_0)$. That shift moves the turn-on to the exact start time without changing the signal shape after the switch.

Use the lesson's boundary convention consistently at the switch instant, and remember the key rule: the step contributes the timing, while the active formula contributes the shape. That is the conversion you will reuse in the next steps.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula at t = 0

example_content.example_prompt: Write a unit-step form for $x(t)=0$ for $t<0$ and $x(t)=2t+1$ for $t\ge 0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a two-case signal with zero before the start and one active formula after the start. Because the switch is at the origin, the gate is $u(t)$.
Keep the active branch exactly as $2t+1$. The step provides the on-off timing; it does not change the formula after $t=0$.
Check the inactive side: for $t<0$, $u(t)=0$, so the whole expression is zero before the start. That matches the original piecewise definition.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula After t = 0

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<2$ and $x(t)=2e^{-t}$ for $t\ge 2$ to a unit-step expression.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a signal that is zero before $t=2$ and follows one active formula after that time. Because the switch happens at $t=2$, the gate is $u(t-2)$.
Keep the active branch exactly as $2e^{-t}$. Only the step argument shifts; the formula itself stays unchanged.
Check both sides: for $t<2$, $u(t-2)=0$, so the expression is zero; for $t\ge 2$, $u(t-2)=1$, so the output is $2e^{-t}$. That matches the piecewise definition.

sections.lesson_title: Starting a Signal with a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Starting an Active Formula Before t = 0

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $x(t)=0$ for $t<-1$ and $x(t)=\sin(t)$ for $t\ge -1$ into a unit-step expression.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a signal that is zero before $t=-1$ and active from $t=-1$ onward. Since the switch turns on one unit before the origin, the gate is $u(t+1)$.
Keep the active branch exactly as $\sin(t)$. Only the step argument changes to reflect the negative start time.
Check both intervals: for $t<-1$, $u(t+1)=0$, so the signal is zero; for $t\ge -1$, $u(t+1)=1$, so the output is $\sin(t)$. That preserves the piecewise definition.

entries.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a delayed exponential into the correct unit-step form e^{a(t - t0)}u(t - t0), recognizing how the shifted step turns the signal on at t0 while the exponential's argument sets the delayed time origin.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Introduction to Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps

blocks.text: A delayed exponential keeps the same exponential shape, but it stays off until the activation time $t_0$. The shifted unit step $u(t-t_0)$ marks that turn-on point, and the shifted argument $t-t_0$ makes the exponential count time from the same delayed origin.

Read the rule as one matched shift: the step decides when the signal turns on, and the exponential decides what time the waveform is measured from after it turns on. If the start time is $t_0=3$, the delayed exponential should use $t-3$ in both places.
The safest recognition rule is simple: do not shift only the step. If the signal starts later, the exponential argument must shift with it so the waveform and the activation time stay aligned.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Delaying a Basic Exponential to a Positive Start Time

example_content.example_prompt: Find the unit-step form for a delayed exponential that starts at $t=3$ and has $e^{-2t}$ shape when active.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delayed exponential: the signal is off before the start time and then follows the same exponential shape after the start time. From the previous step, the matching pattern is to shift both the exponential argument and the unit step by the same amount.
Here the delay is $t_0=3$, so every $t$ in the prototype becomes $t-3$. That gives the same waveform, but its time origin moves to $t=3$ and the step turns the signal on at the same instant.

This is the canonical delayed form: the step handles the activation time, and the shifted exponent handles the delayed time reference. Do not shift only the step, because the exponential itself must move with the same delay.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Including Scale Factors in Delayed Exponential Signals

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $x(t)=3e^{-0.5t}$ delayed by $2$ into unit-step form, and explain how the scale factor $3$ is represented.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same delayed-exponential pattern as before, but now there is a gain of $3$ in front. The delay still belongs in both the exponential argument and the unit step, while the scale factor stays outside the delayed waveform.
Here the delay is $t_0=2$, so every $t$ in the prototype becomes $t-2$. The factor $3$ is unchanged because it is a multiplicative gain, not part of the time shift.

This keeps the active interval and the amplitude separate: for $t<2$ the step is off, and for $t\ge 2$ the signal follows the same delayed exponential shape scaled by $3$. The delay moves the time origin, but the gain stays external.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Converting Piecewise Delayed Exponentials to Step Form

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the piecewise signal $x(t)=\{e^{-t},\,2\le t<7;\,0,\,\text{elsewhere}\}$ to step form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a piecewise exponential with one finite active interval. Since the signal starts at $t=2$, re-anchor the exponential at that start time and use a step difference to gate the interval.
The factor $e^{-2}$ preserves the value at the start time, while $u(t-2)-u(t-7)$ is $1$ only on $2\le t<7$. That combination turns the delayed exponential on at $t=2$ and off at $t=7$.

This matches the piecewise definition exactly: the signal is $0$ before $t=2$, follows the delayed exponential shape on the interval, and returns to $0$ at $t=7$ and beyond. The exponential shift and the two step boundaries are doing separate jobs, so both must appear.

sections.lesson_title: Delaying Exponential Signals with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Distinguishing Delayed Exponentials from Gated Unshifted Exponentials

example_content.example_prompt: For a signal that equals $e^{-t}$ on $2 \le t < 6$ and $0$ elsewhere, write the step form that keeps the waveform unshifted.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite-time window around a formula already written in global time. Because the waveform is specified as $e^{-t}$ itself, do not re-anchor the exponent; just gate the original formula with the interval window.

The step difference is $1$ only on $2\le t<6$, so it preserves the exponential on that interval and kills it outside. If the waveform itself had to move to a new time origin, the exponent would shift too; here it does not.

Quick test: step difference only means gate the existing waveform; shifted exponent plus step means re-time the waveform itself. This prompt is the first case, so the unshifted-gated form is the match.

entries.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
entries.lesson_core_move: Construct rectangular pulses by subtracting appropriately shifted unit step functions to switch a chosen amplitude on at the leading edge and off at the trailing edge.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Introduction to Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps

blocks.text: A rectangular pulse is a signal that is active only over one finite interval and is zero everywhere else. In this lesson, the simplest pulse has unit height, so the main idea is to build that window by turning a signal on and then turning it off.
The unit step is the switch that makes that window possible. A shifted step like $u(t-a)$ turns the signal on at the leading edge $t=a$, and a second shifted step can remove it again at a later time.

Read $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-T)$ as a unit pulse that starts at $t=0$ and ends at $t=T$. The first step creates the leading edge, the subtraction removes the signal at the trailing edge, and the result is 1 only across that finite window.

The same subtraction pattern works for any pulse that begins at $a$ and ends at $b$. The first shifted step marks the leading edge, the second shifted step marks the trailing edge, and their difference gives the rectangular pulse template used in the next examples.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Creating a Unit-Height Pulse from t = 0 to t = T

example_content.example_prompt: Write a unit-height pulse that is on from $t=0$ to $t=T$ and zero elsewhere.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite window with leading edge at $t=0$ and trailing edge at $t=T$. To build that pulse, use the first unit step to turn the signal on at the leading edge and subtract a shifted step to turn it off at the trailing edge.

This difference gives the desired interval behavior. For $t<0$, both steps are 0, so $x(t)=0$. For $0 \le t < T$, the first step is 1 and the second is 0, so $x(t)=1$. For $t \ge T$, both steps are 1, so the subtraction returns to 0. The result is a unit-height pulse on $[0,T)$.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Moving the Pulse Window to Start at t = a

example_content.example_prompt: Create a unit-height pulse that is on for $a \le t < a+T$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same finite window as before, but the leading edge has moved from $t=0$ to $t=a$. To keep the pulse unit height, shift both steps by the same amount so the window starts at $a$ and keeps width $T$.
Set the on-transition to $u(t-a)$ so the signal turns on at the leading edge $t=a$. Then set the off-transition to $u(t-a-T)$ so the signal turns off $T$ units later, at $t=a+T$.

Subtracting the two shifted steps preserves the same rectangular shape while moving the whole window. The result is 0 before $t=a$, 1 on $[a,a+T)$, and 0 again for $t \ge a+T$, so the pulse has the desired start time and unit height.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Scaling the Pulse to a Chosen Amplitude

example_content.example_prompt: Construct $x(t)=3[u(t-1)-u(t-4)]$ and describe its value for each time region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular pulse with the same start and stop times as before, but now the plateau height is $3$ instead of $1$. To scale the pulse correctly, place the coefficient in front of the entire step difference, not on just one step.

The factor $3$ multiplies the whole rectangular pulse. For $t<1$, both steps are 0, so $x(t)=0$. For $1 \le t < 4$, the first step is 1 and the second is 0, so the bracketed difference is 1 and the output is $3$. For $t \ge 4$, both steps are 1, so the difference returns to 0 and the pulse turns off.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Writing a Rectangular Pulse from Its Height and Endpoints

example_content.example_prompt: Write the expression for a pulse of height 4 active between $t=-2$ and $t=5$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular pulse with height $A=4$, starting at $t_1=-2$ and ending at $t_2=5$. Use the standard step-difference form: the first step turns the pulse on at the left endpoint, and the second step turns it off at the right endpoint.
Write the on-switch as $u(t-t_1)=u(t+2)$ and the off-switch as $u(t-t_2)=u(t-5)$. Then place the amplitude multiplier on the whole difference so the pulse keeps height 4 while it is active.

This means the signal is 0 for $t<-2$, equals 4 for $-2\le t<5$, and returns to 0 for $t\ge 5$. The form matches the endpoint specification directly: $u(t+2)$ starts the pulse at $t=-2$, and $u(t-5)$ ends it at $t=5$.

sections.lesson_title: Building Rectangular Pulses with Unit Steps
sections.section_title: Reading the On and Off Times from a Step-Difference Pulse

example_content.example_prompt: From $x(t)=3[u(t+1)-u(t-4)]$, determine where the signal is non-zero and what its non-zero level is.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a step-difference pulse written in the standard form $A[u(t-a)-u(t-b)]$. Read the first step as the on-switch and the second step as the off-switch, then use the leading coefficient as the pulse height.
Here $u(t+1)$ means the pulse turns on at $t=-1$, because $t+1=0$ at that time. Likewise, $u(t-4)$ means the pulse turns off at $t=4$. The coefficient $3$ sets the active level.
So the signal is 0 for $t<-1$, equals 3 for $-1\le t<4$, and returns to 0 for $t\ge 4$. The reverse reading matches the construction rule exactly: first switch on at $t=-1$, then switch off at $t=4$.
